solids-properties-s1.title: Four unknown solids
solids-properties-s1.text: A student tests four white or gray solids, W to Z.

solids-properties-s2.title: Particle views of four solids
solids-properties-s2.html: Key: blue +, cation; green −, anion; gold +, metal cation; small blue dot, electron; line, covalent bond; purple pair, a two-atom molecule.

items.q: Which solid is most likely a molecular solid?
options: X
W
Y
Z

why.correct: X melts low (114 °C), is soft and conducts in neither state. Low melting means only weak intermolecular forces hold the particles together, and no conduction means no ions or free electrons.
options: Right: low melting point, soft, no conduction.
W conducts only when melted, the signature of an ionic solid whose ions become free to move.
Y melts at 1,710 °C, far too high for a solid held by intermolecular forces.
Z conducts as a solid and bends, which marks a metal.

items.q: Which observation best shows that solid W is ionic rather than metallic?
options: W conducts when melted but not as a solid.
W melts at 801 °C, which is higher than the melting points of the common metals found in the periodic table, such as copper and iron.
W is white, while metals have a shiny, silvery color that reflects light from their surfaces.
W is hard, while metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife at room temperature.

why.correct: In an ionic solid the charged particles are held in the lattice, so it cannot conduct until melting or dissolving frees the ions. A metal conducts as a solid because its electrons move freely.
options: Right: conduction only when melted is the ionic signature.
Many metals melt far above 801 °C (iron at 1,538 °C), so melting point does not separate the two.
Color is a weak test, and a powdered metal can look gray or dull.
Most metals are hard; hardness does not tell the two kinds apart. The test is brittleness and conduction.

items.q: Which explanation accounts for solid Y's very high melting point and lack of conductivity?
options: Its atoms form one covalent network, so melting breaks covalent bonds and no charges can move.
Its molecules form many hydrogen bonds to each other, which are strong enough to keep it solid at 1,700 °C.
Its ions are held by very strong ionic bonds, and ions do not carry a current even when the solid has melted into a liquid.
It is a metal whose electrons are held so tightly that they stay put, which raises the melting point.

why.correct: Only breaking covalent bonds explains a melting point near 1,710 °C in a nonconductor. In a covalent network, all valence electrons are in bonds, so nothing carries a charge.
options: Right: a covalent network solid such as quartz.
Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular forces; no molecular solid stays solid anywhere near 1,700 °C.
An ionic solid conducts once melted, and Y does not, so Y is not ionic.
A metal conducts as a solid because of its delocalized electrons; Y does not.

items.q: When solid Z is hammered, it flattens instead of shattering. Which particle-level explanation fits?
options: Layers of cations slide while the electron sea keeps holding them together.
Hammering breaks the covalent bonds between atoms, and new covalent bonds form in the new shape.
Like-charged ions are pushed next to each other, and their repulsion pushes the layers apart.
The intermolecular forces between its molecules are weak, so the molecules move apart and spread out.

why.correct: In a metal the bonding is a sea of electrons shared by all the cations, so shifting a layer does not break it: the metal is malleable.
options: Right: the electron sea moves with the cations, so the solid bends instead of breaking.
Metals are not held by localized covalent bonds, so nothing has to break and re-form.
That repulsion is why ionic solids shatter; Z bends, so it is not ionic.
A molecular solid would crumble, not flatten; Z also conducts, which molecules cannot.

items.q: A fifth solid, V, melts at 186 °C and does not conduct when melted. Which conclusions are supported? Select all that apply.
options: V is a molecular solid.
V's covalent bonds break when it melts.
V contains no free ions or electrons.
V is an ionic solid with small ions.

why.correct: A low melting point means only intermolecular forces hold the particles, so V is molecular, and no conduction when melted means it has no ions or free electrons. (Sucrose fits.)
options: Right: a low melting point points to intermolecular forces between molecules.
Melting a molecular solid overcomes intermolecular forces; its covalent bonds stay intact.
Right: a melted ionic or metallic solid would conduct.
A melted ionic solid conducts, and V does not.

items.q: Which box shows a solid that conducts electricity as a solid?
options: Box 4
Box 2
Box 3
Box 1

why.correct: Box 4 shows metal cations among delocalized electrons. Those electrons move freely, so the solid conducts.
options: Right: mobile electrons carry the current.
The ions in an ionic lattice are fixed, so box 2 conducts only when melted or dissolved.
In a covalent network every electron is in a bond, so nothing carries a charge.
Neutral molecules carry no charge and there are no free electrons.

items.q: Which box best represents solid iodine, I₂?
options: Box 1
Box 2
Box 3
Box 4

why.correct: Iodine is made of separate I₂ molecules. Each pair is joined by a covalent bond, and the pairs are held to each other only by dispersion forces.
options: Right: separate two-atom molecules.
Iodine contains no ions; I₂ is a neutral molecule of one element.
In a network every atom bonds to several neighbours; each iodine atom bonds to just one other.
Iodine is a nonmetal, so it has no cations in a sea of electrons.

items.q: The substance in box 1 melts far lower than the substance in box 3. Which reasoning is correct?
options: Melting box 1 overcomes intermolecular forces; melting box 3 breaks covalent bonds.
The covalent bonds in box 1 are weaker than the covalent bonds in box 3, so they break at a lower temperature.
Box 1 has fewer atoms in the drawing than box 3, so less energy is needed to melt each gram of it.
Box 3 contains ions that attract each other strongly through ionic bonds, while box 1 contains neutral atoms that attract each other far less.

why.correct: Melting a molecular solid pulls whole molecules apart; the bonds within each pair are untouched. Melting a network requires breaking covalent bonds, which takes far more energy.
options: Right: intermolecular forces versus covalent bonds.
Melting box 1 does not break its covalent bonds at all.
The number of atoms drawn is a sampling choice, not a cause of melting point.
Box 3 contains neutral atoms joined by covalent bonds; there are no ions.

items.q: Struck with a hammer, the solid in box 2 shatters. Which explanation is correct?
options: Shifting a layer puts like charges side by side, and they repel.
The delocalized electrons are knocked loose, so nothing holds the cations together.
The intermolecular forces between its molecules are too weak to hold the solid in one piece.
Its covalent bonds are rigid and do not bend, so they snap like twigs when the crystal is struck with a hammer.

why.correct: In an ionic lattice each ion is surrounded by opposite charges. Sliding one layer by one ion lines up + with + and − with −, and the repulsions break the crystal: ionic solids are brittle.
options: Right: repulsion between like charges after a shift.
Box 2 has no delocalized electrons; that describes a metal, which bends instead.
Box 2 contains ions, not molecules, and ionic bonds are strong.
Ionic solids are held by ionic, not covalent, bonds.

items.q: Dry ice, CO₂(s), turns to gas at −78 °C, while quartz, SiO₂(s), melts near 1,710 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
options: Solid CO₂ is molecules held by dispersion forces; quartz is a Si–O covalent network.
Si–O bonds are polar while C=O bonds are not, so quartz molecules attract each other more strongly.
Quartz molecules are heavier than CO₂ molecules, so they need more energy to leave the solid.
Quartz is an ionic solid made of Si⁴⁺ and O²⁻ ions, while CO₂ is made of neutral molecules.

why.correct: The formulas look alike, but CO₂ forms small molecules and SiO₂ forms an endless network. Changing CO₂ to a gas pulls molecules apart; melting quartz breaks Si–O covalent bonds.
options: Right: molecular solid versus covalent network.
C=O bonds are polar too; and quartz has no separate molecules to attract.
Quartz has no separate molecules at all, so molecule mass is the wrong idea.
Si–O bonds are polar covalent, and molten quartz does not conduct like an ionic liquid.

items.q: What holds the particles of a molecular solid to each other?
options: Intermolecular forces
Covalent bonds throughout
Ionic bonds
A sea of electrons

why.correct: The atoms inside each molecule are covalently bonded, but separate molecules are held together by intermolecular forces.
options: Right: attractions between separate molecules.
That describes a covalent network solid.
That describes an ionic solid.
That describes a metallic solid.

items.q: Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon, yet graphite conducts along its layers and diamond does not. Why?
options: In graphite each C bonds to three others and one electron per C is delocalized; in diamond all four are in bonds.
Graphite contains carbon ions, while diamond contains neutral carbon atoms, so graphite has charge carriers.
Diamond's carbon atoms are held by weak intermolecular forces that block the movement of electrons.
Graphite is a metal, because carbon atoms arranged in layers give up their outer electrons the way metal atoms do.

why.correct: Diamond uses all four valence electrons of each C in localized bonds. Graphite uses three; the remaining electrons spread over the whole sheet and can move along it.
options: Right: delocalized electrons within each graphite layer.
Both contain neutral carbon atoms; there are no carbon ions.
Diamond is a covalent network held entirely by covalent bonds.
Graphite is a covalent network with delocalized electrons, not a metal.

items.q: A clear solid softens gradually from 550 °C to 700 °C instead of melting at one temperature. What does this best suggest?
options: It is an amorphous solid, with no long-range order.
It is a crystalline molecular solid whose molecules melt together at one time.
It is an ionic solid whose ions are beginning to conduct electricity.
It is impure, because a pure crystalline solid has no melting point.

why.correct: A crystal's ordered pattern gives every particle the same environment, so it melts sharply. In an amorphous solid like glass the environments vary, so it softens over a range.
options: Right: gradual softening marks an amorphous solid such as glass.
Molecules all melting at once would give a sharp melting point, not a range.
Conductivity says nothing about whether melting is sharp or gradual.
A pure crystalline solid has a sharp melting point; it does not lack one.

items.q: Put these solids in order of melting point, lowest first.
options: Solid CH₄ (methane)
Ice, H₂O
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Diamond, C

why.correct: Methane (−182 °C) is molecular with dispersion forces only; ice (0 °C) is molecular with hydrogen bonds; NaCl (801 °C) is ionic; diamond (above 3,500 °C) is a covalent network.

items.q: Which substances form molecular solids? Select all that apply.
options: Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁
Silicon carbide, SiC
Potassium bromide, KBr
Solid carbon dioxide, CO₂
Copper, Cu

why.correct: Sucrose and CO₂ are made of separate molecules. SiC is a covalent network, KBr is ionic and copper is metallic.
options: Right: separate sucrose molecules.
SiC is a hard covalent network like diamond.
KBr is a metal with a nonmetal: an ionic solid.
Right: separate CO₂ molecules (dry ice).
Copper is a metal: cations in a sea of electrons.

items.q: Naphthalene (C₁₀H₈, melts at 80 °C) and urea (CO(NH₂)₂, melts at 133 °C) are both molecular solids. Urea's molar mass (60.06 g/mol) is less than half of naphthalene's (128.17 g/mol). Which claim best explains urea's higher melting point?
options: Urea molecules hydrogen-bond through their N–H groups; naphthalene cannot.
Urea is a covalent network solid, so melting it breaks covalent bonds between the molecules in the crystal.
Urea molecules have more electrons than naphthalene molecules, so their dispersion forces are stronger.
Urea is ionic because it contains nitrogen, so its melting point lies between those of salts and molecules.

why.correct: Naphthalene is nonpolar (dispersion only, 68 electrons). Urea has only 32 electrons, but its N–H hydrogens bond to the O and N lone pairs of neighbours. Hydrogen bonding outweighs the smaller dispersion forces.
options: Right: hydrogen bonds explain it, not mass.
The question states urea is molecular; 133 °C is far too low for a network.
Urea has 32 electrons and naphthalene 68, so dispersion favours naphthalene.
Urea is made of neutral molecules; containing N does not make a compound ionic.

items.q: A student claims: "Ice melts at 0 °C because the O–H bonds in water break at that temperature." Which is the best correction?
options: Melting overcomes hydrogen bonds between molecules; the O–H bonds stay intact.
Ice melts because its ionic bonds break, releasing H⁺ and OH⁻ ions into the liquid that forms.
The claim is correct for ice, because ice is a covalent network solid of O–H bonds.
Ice melts because its dispersion forces break, while the hydrogen bonds stay intact in liquid water.

why.correct: Ice is a molecular solid. Liquid water is still made of H₂O molecules, so no O–H bond broke; hydrogen bonds between molecules were partly overcome.
options: Right: melting a molecular solid overcomes attractions between molecules.
Water molecules are covalent, not ionic; melting does not form ions.
Ice is molecular: separate H₂O molecules held by hydrogen bonds.
Melting loosens all the attractions between molecules, including many hydrogen bonds.
